title: Is USMNT a legit World Cup contender? Have fans cracked the cheap-ticket code? Day 2 Recap
content:
After all the talking, all the controversies, all the expectations, the U.S. men’s national team began their home tournament with possibly the best half of soccer in their World Cup history, seizing a 3-0 lead over Paraguay that they converted into a 4-1 win.

The star man was Monaco’s Folarin Balogun, with two goals, before Gio Reyna — almost sent home from Qatar four years ago over disciplinary issues — scored the goal of the tournament thus far.

One concern, however, and a big one: Star winger Christian Pulisic was withdrawn at half-time as a precaution after feeling tightness in his calf. He had looked electric in the first 45 minutes. Now, a nation holds its breath.

Elsewhere, co-hosts Canada rescued a deserved late draw amid an electric atmosphere in Toronto, securing their first-ever World Cup point.

And the day began with significant news for Ghana, with The Athletic revealing that starting midfielder Thomas Partey was denied entry to Canada due to ongoing rape and sexual assault charges that the former Arsenal midfielder is facing in the UK; he denies all the charges. This means he will not be allowed to feature against Panama on June 17.

The Athletic will provide daily recaps of the World Cup’s biggest talking points throughout the tournament. This is what happened on Matchday 2.

Job done — and in style. Four goals, the most ever scored by the USMNT in World Cup history, and a first-half performance that will go down as their best 45 minutes in a major tournament.

What a time to do it, amid the drama of the build-up. The question is no longer whether this side can compete at their home World Cup; it has shifted quickly to how far they can go.

Mauricio Pochettino will be able to put a cross in virtually every box on his checklist after that performance — Pulisic’s fitness pending.

Pochettino’s striker, Balogun, appears in top form, with an especially clinical weaker left foot finish for his second. The U.S. midfield ran the game, particularly through Malik Tillman’s uber-intensity. And Pochettino’s defence, until Mauricio’s 73rd-minute consolation, was largely untroubled; that goal was Paraguay’s only shot on target.

Pochettino’s one concern will be the fitness of Pulisic, who looked sharp before being withdrawn as a precaution at half-time with a calf complaint. The USMNT won easily without their star player carrying the load, but against teams better than a poor Paraguay, his intelligence, energy and skill will be required.

“I don’t think it’s anything,” the winger told reporters after the match, likely crossing his fingers.

So, with a coach with real knockout pedigree and a squad with strength at every level, just how far can this side go? The Athletic’s live projections give the USMNT a 97 per cent chance of advancing to the knockouts, with a 59 per cent chance of winning their group.

Should the USMNT do that, they will face the runner-up from one of Groups B, E, F, I and J (potentially teams such as Canada, Ecuador, Japan, Senegal and Austria). The latter three are especially tricky opponents, but the USMNT sit higher than all five in the world rankings.

If they finish second in their group (a 31 per cent chance), the runner-up of Group G will be next, which has a high likelihood of being Iran. Though this might arguably be an easier fixture in the round of 32, this pathway would lead to more difficult matches from the round of 16 on.

Still, all that excitement has us getting ahead of ourselves. The USMNT next plays Australia in Seattle on Friday.

“No one can see a bubble,” Ryan Gosling’s character, Jared Vennett, says in the 2015 film “The Big Short.” “That’s what makes it a bubble.”

In the build-up to this tournament, FIFA’s pricing strategy has been under fire. It is the most expensive World Cup in history, with the governing body’s dynamic pricing model meaning many tickets in equivalent areas have more than doubled in price from four years ago.

With swaths of empty seats Thursday night during the tournament’s second game in Guadalajara, fans appeared to show their discontent with their feet.

But with dynamic pricing, what goes up can also go down, and several wily USMNT fans have proved Vennett’s quote is not quite true.

The Athletic’s Henry Bushnell has been covering FIFA’s ticketing issues for months, spending much of his Friday wandering around SoFi Stadium’s concourse, canvassing fans. Several of them let him onto their secret.

One father and son explained how they bought premium, 200-level tickets on Gametime for $1,300 each, and while that might sound dear, that purchase was made at less than half of FIFA’s original price.

Another family, from Texas, took a last-minute opportunity to secure tickets when the father, Tony, who had been tracking prices over recent weeks, seized on an opportunity via a resale site. His four tickets cost a total of $5,000 ($1,250 each), which is once more less than half the original price.

Gianni Infantino said at his pre-tournament news conference that demand at the listed prices had been tenfold — but many fans have called that bluff and reaped the rewards. They might not be so successful next Friday against Australia, as prices have spiked once again after the fervor of the USMNT’s big win.

Drums, flares and a sea of red: Mexico does not have a monopoly on fan passion at this World Cup.

Canada’s fan march through downtown Toronto before the opening match was a remarkable sight, and after their side trailed Bosnia-Herzegovina for almost an hour, that support was rewarded.

Jesse Marsch opted to bring on Southampton striker Cyle Larin with 12 minutes remaining, and it took just 121 seconds for his decision to be justified, as the 31 year old  brilliantly converted a clever flicked pass from Promise David.

The goal secured Canada’s men their first points in World Cup history, having lost all three games four years ago.

With matches remaining against Switzerland and Qatar, Canada’s draw means The Athletic’s supercomputer forecasts them to now have an 88 per cent chance of progression to the knockout stages, with Larin’s goal boosting those chances by roughly 13 per cent.

Fans of Larin’s former club, Real Valladolid, invented the phrase “Larinisimo” to honor the forward’s exploits — it might just be time to dust off that moniker for summer.

Four games in 11 hours. With the host-nation festivities out of the way, Saturday feels like the meat of the tournament proper. After positive results for all three hosts, now we’re cooking with gas.

The day begins with 2022 hosts Qatar facing knockout stalwarts Switzerland. The Swiss will be heavy favourites. Though Qatar has impressed at the Asian Football Confederation level, it disappointed on the big stage four years ago. Watch out for 20-year-old Swiss midfielder Johan Manzambi, who has been brilliant for Freiburg in Germany this season; he could be one of the stars of this tournament.

Next up is one of the ties of the knockout stages, as AFCON champion Morocco (winner of the title in contested circumstances after initial winner Senegal was disqualified retrospectively after leaving the pitch in protest) take on Brazil, the most successful men’s World Cup side of all time, with five titles.

Morocco was a surprise semi-finalist at the last World Cup after knocking out Spain and Portugal on the way. The North African nation retains much of the same squad, which has arguably aged into their prime. They will co-host the tournament in four years with Portugal and Spain.

After a rocky period for Brazil in recent years, legendary coach Carlo Ancelotti has steadied the ship. His side boasts global superstars such as Vinicius Junior (Real Madrid) and Raphinha (Barcelona), though Neymar will miss the first game with injury. The Selecao could go all the way.

Scotland are set to boast some of the loudest fans in the tournament — the Tartan Army — who will celebrate their first World Cup in 28 years against World Cup debutants Haiti in Foxborough. The Scots will be hoping Serie A Player of the Year in 2024-25, Scott McTominay, has recovered from an upset stomach; the Napoli midfielder is his side’s talisman.

Rounding out the day on Canada’s west coast is the rest of the USMNT’s group, as Australia meets Turkey; both sides will have designs on reaching the knockouts. Arda Guler is the latter’s key man, and the 21-year-old Real Madrid attacker is possibly the best ball-striker at the tournament. Watch out if he gets the ball anywhere within 30 yards.

Group B: Qatar vs Switzerland (3pm ET; 8pm BST)
Group C: Brazil vs Morocco (6pm ET; 11pm BST)
Group C: Haiti vs Scotland (9pm ET; 2am BST)
Group D: Australia vs Turkey (9pm PT; 12am ET; 5am BST)
